name: Draksharama Bhimeswara Temple
period: Eastern Chalukya of Vengi (Bhima I), c. 9th–10th century
summary: One of the five Pancharama Kshetras, this great temple at Draksharama enshrines Shiva as Bhimeswara around a towering lingam, and shares its ground with the Manikyamba Shakti Peetha — Shiva and the Goddess honoured together in the Godavari delta.

sections.history: Draksharama rises in the fertile Godavari delta of the Konaseema country, and its great shrine to Bhimeswara was raised by the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi — the work is credited to Bhima I in the ninth to tenth centuries, from whom the deity takes his name. Built as a two-storeyed structure around an unusually tall lingam, the temple has been honoured and enriched by successive rulers of the Telugu land. Its old Telugu inscriptions are among the treasures of the site, and it has long stood as one of the most revered Shiva kshetras of coastal Andhra.
sections.architecture: The temple is laid out as a large walled complex with a two-tiered sanctum built around a lingam so tall that it is worshipped from an upper gallery as well as from the ground. Broad pillared halls, carved stone, and old inscriptions line the enclosure, and a stepped tank stands within the grounds. The Eastern Chalukya builders gave the shrine a massive, foursquare dignity rather than a soaring tower, and the sense on entering is of great age and solidity — the lingam pale and immense in the dim inner shrine.
sections.legends: Draksharama is counted among the five Pancharama Kshetras, born of the lingam that the demon Tarakasura wore at his throat: when Kumara Swamy slew the demon the lingam broke into five pieces, and one came to rest here to be fixed and consecrated by the gods. The site is also revered as the Manikyamba Shakti Peetha, one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas, where the Goddess is worshipped as Manikyamba — so Shiva as Bhimeswara and the Goddess share the sacred ground. The seven sages, the Saptarishis, are remembered as having drawn the Godavari here in seven streams, giving the region its holiness.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple’s greatest night, when the delta streams toward Bhimeswara through the small hours. The annual kalyanam, the sacred marriage of god and goddess, is celebrated with great festivity, and the Devi’s own observances at the Manikyamba shrine draw Shakta pilgrims especially through Navaratri. Karthika Masam, the lunar month dear to Shiva, fills the temple with lamps and devotees.
sections.experience: To stand before the towering pale lingam of Bhimeswara, lit by lamplight in the old two-storeyed shrine, is to feel the weight of more than a thousand years. Pilgrims move between the god’s sanctum and the Goddess Manikyamba nearby, taking in both in a single visit, and pause at the stepped tank and the long inscribed walls. Set among the green paddy of the Godavari delta, Draksharama keeps the unhurried, deeply rooted air of a great country kshetra.

visit.timings: Generally open early morning to around midday and again from late afternoon to night; darshan hours extend on Shivaratri and festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not permitted inside the sanctum; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Draksharamam is in the Konaseema district of the Godavari delta, about 30 km from Kakinada and reachable by road from Rajahmundry; the nearest airport is Rajahmundry, with Visakhapatnam the larger gateway.
